title: Solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance search for axion-like dark matter with broadband SQUID magnetometry
authors: Andrew J. Winter, János Ádám, Deniz Aybas, Dmitry Budker, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Surjeet Rajendran, Arne Wickenbrock, Alexander O. Sushkov
abstract: We report the results of an experimental search for ultralight axion-like dark matter in the mass ranges 19.5--20.5 and 21.5--22 neV. The Cosmic Axion Spin Precession Experiment-electric probes the axion-nuclear electric dipole moment coupling. We perform solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance on $^{207}$Pb spin ensembles which reside in a polarized ferroelectric crystal. The background axion-like dark matter field induces an oscillating torque on the $^{207}$Pb spins via the electric dipole moment coupling $g_{d}$. The experiment is calibrated with pulsed magnetic resonance measurements covering two frequency bands (4.6--5.0 and 5.2--5.3 MHz) that correspond to the axion Compton frequencies associated with the identified axion mass ranges. By sweeping the leading magnetic field applied to the sample, we are able to detect the $^{207}$Pb nuclear magnetic resonance in these frequency ranges using a superconducting quantum interference device, inductively coupled to the sample with a broadband circuit. We establish the upper bounds $|g_{d}| < 4\times 10^{-4}$ GeV$^{-2}$ with 95% confidence in these frequency bands. Our results demonstrate the detection and small-tip angle calibration of low-field $^{207}$Pb nuclear magnetic resonance, allowing for sensitivity to axion-like dark matter in the nanoelectron-volt axion mass range.
summary: This experiment searches for ultralight axion-like dark matter by measuring the oscillating torque it induces on nuclear spins in a solid-state system. Using broadband SQUID magnetometry on polarized $^{207}	ext{Pb}$, the researchers successfully calibrated their setup and set stringent upper bounds on the axion-nuclear electric dipole coupling constant. The results demonstrate a highly sensitive technique for probing fundamental physics in the nanoelectron-volt mass range.
main_problem: The paper reports an experimental search for ultralight axion-like dark matter (ALPs) by looking for its coupling to the electric dipole moment of atomic nuclei.

method: The measurement uses solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) on polarized $^{207}	ext{Pb}$ spins, detecting the oscillating torque induced by the ambient axion field using a superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID).
model_or_system: The system involves $^{207}	ext{Pb}$ spins polarized in a ferroelectric crystal, interacting with the axion field via an electric dipole moment coupling ($H_{EDM}$). The detection relies on measuring the induced oscillating magnetization ($M_{xy}$) coupled to the SQUID.

paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical basis of the EDM coupling, describes the experimental setup using SQUID magnetometry on polarized $^{207}	ext{Pb}$, outlines the calibration procedure using pulsed NMR, and finally presents the derived upper bounds on the axion-nucleon coupling constant.
why_interesting: This work bridges condensed matter techniques (solid-state NMR, SQUID magnetometry) with fundamental particle physics searches (axion dark matter), providing a highly sensitive, low-frequency measurement platform relevant to quantum sensing.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Experimental setup schematic. Top: the CASPEr-electric apparatus schematic. A polarized ferroelectric PMN-PT sample is placed inside a superconducting magnet bore. The static magnetic field Bz and the ferroelectric polarization vector Pr are orthogonal to each other. An excitation coil and a separate pickup coil are wound around the sample. The latter is coupled to a SQUID, which resides within a niobium superconducting shield. The whole setup is immersed in liquid helium. Bottom: electronic circuit schematics. The digital to analog converter (DAC) delivers a pulse to the SRS SIM954 amplifier (A) with a gain factor of 4. A transformer with primary and secondary coils Ltr1 and Ltr2...

FIG. 2: Pulsed NMR sequence used for calibration FID measurements. The equilibrium magnetization of the spin ensemble is initially parallel to the leading field B0. An RF excitation pulse tips the magnetization into the transverse plane by an angle θ. The resulting FID signal is due to the spin ensemble precessing about the leading field as the transverse component decays.

FIG. 3: Calibration measurements. a. Real and imaginary quadratures of the Fourier-transformed free induction decay data (20 averages) for 207Pb free induction decay in a PMN-PT single crystal, taken at the Larmor frequency f0 ≈4697 kHz. The data are modeled with Lorentzian lineshapes, the resulting best-fit FWHM linewidth is FWHM = Γ/π = 9 kHz. b. The dependence of FID amplitude on pulse duration. The linear behavior confirms the small-tip angle regime. c. The gradual saturation of nuclear spin magnetization by a series of small tip angle excitation pulses. The magnitude of each pulse tip angle θ is extracted from the A0 cosN θ fit model. d. The calibration of magnetic resonance detection...

FIG. 4: The 207Pb excitation spectrum λ(ω). The leading magnetic field was held constant, corresponding to the Larmor frequency 4639 kHz, while 40 µs-long RF excitation pulses of varying frequencies were used to excite the spin FID. We model the spectrum as a Lorentzian (red, dashed line), normalized such that the area under the fit is unity.

FIG. 5: The histogram of the data obtained after performing matched filtering on the data taken at the Larmor frequency of 4757 kHz. The histogram is modeled as a normal distribution (red line). Black, dashed line: 95 % confidence limit for a 5σ detection, indicating the minimum threshold to be considered an ALP candidate.
